title: Three-Week IB Computer Science Revision Plan
summary: IB Computer Science revision plan for November: triage topics, practise questions, complete timed papers and protect rest across three focused weeks.
body_markdown:
November revision has an unusual pressure. The exams are close enough to feel urgent, yet Computer Science is rarely the only subject asking for your attention.


A useful **IB Computer Science revision plan** does not attempt to relearn the entire course in three weeks. It identifies where marks are being lost, repairs the most important gaps, and gradually shifts from learning to timed performance. You should still leave room for your other subjects and for sleep.


This plan is designed for the syllabus examined in the November 2026 session. Check your personal exam schedule and confirm the papers required for your level with your school. The IB's new Computer Science course is first assessed in May 2027, so students sitting in November 2026 remain on the preceding assessment structure.


### Your three-week overview


Week Main priority Suggested Computer Science workload Outcome


Week 1 Diagnose and rebuild 45-75 minutes on 5 days Ranked topic list and repaired foundations


Week 2 Apply and connect 60-90 minutes on 5 days Better question selection, explanations and pseudocode


Week 3 Rehearse and recover 2-3 timed papers plus light review Stable timing and a rested exam-day routine


Adjust those blocks around your full November calendar. If Mathematics or another demanding subject falls near Computer Science, shorten the daily sessions rather than borrowing from sleep. Three attentive 45-minute blocks usually offer more value than one exhausted late-night marathon.


### Before week one: build a revision map


Begin with evidence, not instinct. Students often revise the topic that feels most familiar because familiarity is comforting. The exam, unfortunately, rewards what you can retrieve and apply across the whole assessed course.


Take one representative set of questions under light time pressure. Do not revise immediately beforehand. Mark each response and classify every lost mark:


- **Knowledge:** you could not recall the concept or terminology.
- **Application:** you knew the content but could not apply it to the scenario.
- **Technique:** your answer was vague, incomplete or poorly matched to the command term.
- **Timing:** you could have answered but ran out of time.
- **Carelessness:** you misread data, skipped a subpart or failed to trace an algorithm accurately.


Now label each syllabus area red, amber or green. Red means weak and frequently assessed. Amber means inconsistent. Green means dependable, not merely familiar. Your plan should spend roughly half its topic-review time on red areas, a third on amber areas and the remainder checking green ones.


This map prevents a common mistake: treating every chapter as equally urgent. Revision is resource allocation. Time spent polishing a secure definition is time unavailable for repairing a weak trace table or network explanation.


### Week one: repair the foundations


The first week of IB Computer Science revision is for rebuilding knowledge you will need repeatedly. Focus on core topics, your prescribed option, and the additional HL material if you are an HL student. HL students should also schedule distinct preparation for the case study rather than allowing it to disappear inside general review.


A practical five-session pattern is:


- **Session 1:** systems fundamentals and computer organisation
- **Session 2:** networks, databases or another red core area
- **Session 3:** computational thinking, logic and pseudocode
- **Session 4:** your option topic
- **Session 5:** HL extension or a mixed retrieval check


For each session, use a short cycle: retrieve, check, practise, record. Start by writing what you remember without notes. Then correct the gaps with concise **Study Notes** and convert stubborn facts into **Flashcards** . Finish with targeted questions in the **RevisionDojo Questionbank** .


Keep an error log with four columns: topic, mistake, correct reasoning and next review date. “Revise databases” is too vague to guide tomorrow's work. “Confused primary and foreign keys in a relational schema” gives you something precise to fix.


Do not spend this week producing beautiful summaries. Notes can create a feeling of progress while leaving recall untouched. If you cannot explain a concept without looking down, it is not secure yet.


### Week two: turn knowledge into marks


Week two changes the question from “Do I know this?” to “Can I use it when the wording changes?”


Work with mixed question sets rather than staying inside one comfortable chapter. Alternating topics forces you to identify the method independently, which is closer to the decision-making required in an exam. Use the Questionbank to target weak skills, then use RevisionDojo's **AI Chat** when a mark scheme or pseudocode step needs clarification. Treat the explanation as a starting point and verify it against your teacher's guidance and the relevant course materials.


Pay particular attention to three forms of performance.


### Write to the command term


A definition needs precision. An explanation needs a reasoned connection. A comparison needs both sides. An evaluation requires a supported judgement, not a list of disconnected advantages and disadvantages.


After marking a response, rewrite only the sentence that failed to earn the mark. This is faster and more instructive than copying a complete model answer.


### Trace before you code


When an algorithm feels confusing, slow down. Record variable values systematically, follow each condition, and count loop iterations. For pseudocode questions, test your proposed logic with a normal input and an edge case. A solution that looks elegant but fails on an empty list or boundary value is not finished.


### Practise the required paper formats


Use official specimen material and authorised previous-session questions that match your syllabus. Complete sections under partial timing before attempting whole papers. SL and HL students face different requirements, while HL students also need focused case-study preparation. Follow the timings and structure supplied by your school and the official materials for your session.


By the weekend, review your error log. A mistake that appears three times is no longer a small accident. Give it a dedicated repair block in week three.


A student asks whether debugging can wait while a bouncer representing sleep guards the bed.


### Week three: rehearse the exam, then taper


The final week is not a contest to see how many hours you can survive. It is a rehearsal followed by a taper.


Complete 2-3 full timed papers or paper sections in RevisionDojo's **Exam mode** , depending on your timetable and level. Reproduce exam conditions: clear desk, correct time limit, no notes, no messages and no pausing when a question becomes uncomfortable.


Mark the work with the available guidance and use **Grading tools** to spot omissions or unclear explanations. A score matters, but the diagnosis matters more. Ask:


- Did I allocate time according to the available marks?
- Which command terms produced incomplete responses?
- Where did I lose time without making progress?
- Did I show intermediate reasoning in algorithm questions?
- Which errors could I realistically prevent next time?


If a **Predicted Paper** or **Mock Exam** is available for your course, use it as an additional rehearsal, not as a forecast of exact questions. Its purpose is to test breadth, timing and composure.


During the final 48 hours, reduce intensity. Review your compact error log, essential terminology, common pseudocode patterns and any teacher-directed case-study material. Avoid opening a large new topic unless it is a serious, high-priority gap. The goal is accessible knowledge, not one more exhausted hour at the desk.


### Make the plan work alongside other IB subjects


A November student may have several exams compressed into a short period. Plan at Diploma level, not one subject at a time.


Place every exam on one calendar. Give the nearest and weakest subjects the largest blocks, then maintain Computer Science with shorter retrieval sessions until its final focused phase. A realistic day might contain one 75-minute priority block, one 45-minute secondary block and one 20-minute recall session.


Protect at least one lighter evening each week. Keep exercise, meals and sleep in the timetable as fixed commitments. Rest is not time stolen from revision. It is part of the system that lets you retrieve, reason and check your work when the clock is running.


### The plan is a feedback loop


A strong plan is not rigid. At the end of each day, ask what changed. If networks move from red to amber, shift time elsewhere. If timed practice reveals weak algorithm tracing, bring that topic forward. The calendar should respond to evidence.


RevisionDojo brings that feedback loop into one place. Use the **Questionbank** for targeted practice, **Study Notes** and **Flashcards** for retrieval, and **AI Chat** when an explanation needs another angle. Then move into **Exam mode** for timed papers, supported by grading tools, Predicted Papers and Mock Exams. The **Coursework Library** and specialist **Tutors** can support the wider course when relevant, but these last three weeks should remain centred on the assessed tasks ahead.


Start with one diagnostic set today. Build the map. Repair what matters. Then practise under the conditions in which the knowledge must eventually perform.
